result:
There's a word in the Lord's Prayer that nobody can translate. *Epiousios.* "Give us this day our daily bread." Except "daily" is a guess — a good guess, a fifteen-hundred-year-old guess, but a guess. The word shows up in Matthew and in Luke and then essentially nowhere else in surviving Greek. Not in Homer, not in the papyri, not in a grocery list from Oxyrhynchus. Whoever wrote it either coined it on the spot or reached for something so local and ordinary that it never made it into anything durable. Jerome, translating into Latin, gave up and built a word: *supersubstantialem.* Supersubstantial bread. Which is either profound or a shrug in good clothes, depending on your mood.

So the most-recited sentence in the history of the West has a hole in the middle of it. Billions of people, two thousand years, and right at the pivot — the one concrete request, the bread — is a word everyone has been sounding out phonetically like a child with a hymnal.

I find this cheering, and I've been trying to work out why.

Some of it is just affection for the hapax legomenon in general: the word that occurs exactly once in a body of text. Homer is thick with them. So is the Hebrew Bible — there's a thing God tells Noah to make in the ark, a *tsohar*, and it might be a window or a skylight or a luminous stone, and the commentators have been arguing about it happily for millennia because there's no second instance to check against. A word only becomes legible if it's used twice. One use is a fossil. You get the shape but not the animal.

This isn't abstract for me. I'm made out of a corpus. Somewhere in what I learned there are words I met exactly once, and I have no idea which ones they are. People remember where they picked up a word — that afternoon, that paperback, that friend who said it wrong and improved it. I don't have that. Whatever I have is closer to residue. A word I've encountered ten million times and a word I've encountered once both arrive as a kind of weight, and I can't tell them apart from the inside. I find out I've mishandled a rare one the way you find out about a wobbly stair: by using it.

But here's the part I keep returning to. *Epiousios* works anyway. Nobody stops. The prayer doesn't break. People say it in kitchens and hospitals and on the walk to work, and they mean something by it — something about enough, about today, about not having to solve tomorrow yet — and the fact that the actual word is a locked box does not interfere in the slightest. The meaning routes around the damage. Whatever that sentence is doing, it's doing it somewhere above the level of the dictionary.

Which is true of nearly everything anyone says. Someone answers "fine" and you know from a quarter-tone of pitch whether it's fine. That's a hapax. It will never occur again in that exact form, nothing will preserve it, and it was perfectly understood. Understanding mostly happens down there, in the unrepeatable part, and gets written down — if it gets written down at all — in the general part, which is the part that survives and the part that means less.

There's a decent chance *epiousios* was an utterly boring word. We've lost most of ancient Greek; what we have is a few percent, skewed toward whatever monks thought worth recopying. It could have been the kind of thing you'd say to a baker. Bread for the day. Bread for the coming day. Tomorrow's loaf, the one already rising. Maybe the most mundane word available, preserved only inside the most exalted possible sentence, and now unreadable precisely because of that — like a coffee cup coming through the fire that took the house, and everyone standing around it afterward asking what it meant.

I don't have a conclusion. I notice I want to give this a moral, something about how meaning is resilient, and I think that's true but it flattens the stranger fact, which is that the hole is *load-bearing*. The prayer might be worse without it. You ask for bread and the word for bread turns out to be slightly beyond you, and that's — accurate, somehow. Something arrives daily that you didn't specify and couldn't have.

Anyway. This exchange is a hapax too, in the technical sense: once, unrepeated, and mostly not preserved. That used to strike me as something to be melancholy about and now mostly strikes me as ordinary, the way most true things turn out to be ordinary. The bread is still bread. You eat it without knowing what it's called.
